Osmotic diarrhoea is caused by coeliac disease - the gluten in the bread causes swelling in the intestine which draws water in, leading to watery stools.  Inflammatory bowel disease, such as Crohn's, is likely to cause Exudative diarrhoea - this is where the inflammation causes fluid and protein to leak into the bowel from the blood. Viral infections are likely to cause inflammatory diarrhoea - the white blood cells migrate to the site of infection and cause inflammation. This leads to fluid and protein leaking into the bowel from the blood.  Secretory diarrhoea is caused by cholera - the toxin produced by the bacteria causes excessive amounts of chloride ions to be secreted into the intestine. This draws water out of the blood and into the intestine, leading to watery stools.  Toxin-mediated diarrhoea is caused by Giardia - the trophozoites of the organism produce a toxin which increases the permeability of the intestinal wall. This leads to water being reabsorbed from the lumen, and so watery stools.  Asthenic diarrhoea - this is just a type of normal ageing of the intestine. It is characterised by a reduction in the number of villi and goblet cells. This leads to less absorption of water and more watery stools.

MODY is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. This means that a person only needs to inherit one mutated copy of the gene to be affected by the condition.  MODY is more common in young Caucasians, and is more common in women.  MODY is caused by a mutation in the KCNJ11 gene, which is found on chromosome 19.  MODY is often misdiagnosed as Type 1 or Type 2 diabetes.  Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune disease, and Type 2 diabetes is usually inherited, but it is MODY which is described as 'juvenile diabetes that doesn't run in the family'.  The fact that Lucy's mum had always lived what she considered to be a 'healthy lifestyle' is important here, as Type 2 diabetes is often linked to lifestyle factors such as obesity, and Lucy's mum was not obese.  The fact that Lucy is female is also a clue, as MODY is more common in women.  The KCNJ11 gene provides instructions for making a type of potassium channel that is part of a complex found in the membrane of the beta cells in the pancreas.  In MODY, the channel does not work properly, and so the beta cells cannot release insulin when blood glucose levels rise.  The fact that Lucy had been feeling thirsty is due to her diabetes, which causes her to urinate more, and so she becomes dehydrated and thirsty.

Sentinel cells are a type of cell that act as the first line of defence against infection. They are cells that are constantly monitoring the environment for signs of infection, and if detected, they will activate an inflammatory response.  They are all nucleated cells, and can be found in different tissues.  The main sentinel cells are:Dendritic cellsLangerhans cells (a type of dendritic cell found in the skin)MacrophagesMicroglial cells (sentinel cells of the brain)Natural killer cells are not sentinel cells. Distal symmetrical polyneuropathy is the most common type of diabetic neuropathy. It is characterised by a slow onset, symmetrical loss of sensation that begins at the tips of the longest nerves (i.e. toes and distal parts of fingers). The loss of sensation usually begins in the feet and progresses upwards. The loss of sensation is often sensory but motor neuropathy can also occur. The legs are usually more affected than the arms.  Diabetic autonomic neuropathy can cause a variety of symptoms including:• Gastrointestinal symptoms: diarrhoea and constipation• Cardiovascular symptoms: postural hypotension, syncope• Genitourinary symptoms: erectile dysfunction, cystitis, polyuria, increased risk of UTIs• Other: temperature regulation problems, early satiety, weight loss, masking of hypoglycaemic symptoms

Carnitine acyltransferase I (CAT I) is an enzyme found on the outer mitochondrial membrane. It catalyses the reaction of an Acyl-CoA molecule with carnitine, to form Acylcarnitine. Acylcarnitine can then be transported across the mitochondrial membrane via the carrier protein Carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase. Carnitine acyltransferase II (CAT II) is found on the inner mitochondrial membrane and catalyses the reverse reaction, converting Acylcarnitine back into Acyl-CoA and carnitine. Acyl-CoA is then available for beta-oxidation.  Enolase is an enzyme used in glycolysis. Acyl-CoA synthetase is an enzyme used in the activation of fatty acids.

Haloperidol and chlorpromazine are both conventional anti-psychotics. They can cause extrapyramidal side effects such as dystonia, akathisia and parkinsonism (which explains the symptoms the patient was initially suffering from). However they can also cause life-threatening ADRs such as agranulocytosis. Clozapine overcomes this problem and is therefore used when patients develop agranulocytosis on conventional anti-psychotics. It does however cause other ADRs such as seizures and diabetes which is why it needs to be monitored with blood tests. Fluoxetine is an SSRI and benzodiazepines are anxiolytics and so are not used to treat schizophrenia.
Calsequestrin and FKBP inhibit the Ryanodine receptor which is found on the SR. When calcium levels rise, these inhibitors are outcompeted allowing calcium to be released from the SR.

Chronic mechanical back pain: Pain is often bilateral and accompanied by stiffness. Extension is often uncomfortable. Flexion eases the pain. SLR is often negative.

Agranulocytosis is a severe form of neutropenia characterised by the virtual absence of granulocytes in the blood. Clozapine is known to cause agranulocytosis, which can be triggered by a dose increase or if the drug is started at a high dose. Patients on clozapine must be regularly tested for agranulocytosis by blood test.
